themes.name: Why neurons are hard to read
themes.summary: The paper starts from a problem it did not create: individual MLP neurons fire on mixtures of unrelated things, so reading a network neuron by neuron does not work. Its explanation for that is superposition, a hypothesis carried over from the authors' earlier toy models, in which a network packs more features than it has neurons by giving each feature its own direction rather than its own coordinate. This theme sets out the unit the paper wants instead — a feature, understood as a direction in activation space — and the three criteria it says a good decomposition has to meet. It comes first because everything later is an attempt to produce such a decomposition and then argue that it worked.

sections.title: Comparing features between two one-layer transformers

themes.name: The model and the autoencoder
themes.summary: Two models are involved, and keeping them apart matters for everything that follows. One is the subject: a one-layer transformer with a 512-neuron MLP, overtrained on the Pile, whose MLP activations are the thing being decomposed. The other is the tool: a sparse autoencoder, wider than the layer it reads, trained to rebuild those activations from a small number of active hidden units, with an L1 penalty doing the work of forcing most units to zero. This theme also covers the training details the paper singles out as mattering — the tied pre-encoder bias, resampling of dead neurons — and the notation used to name a feature.

themes.name: Four features up close
themes.summary: Having a decomposition is not the same as having interpretable features, so the paper picks four — Arabic script, DNA, base64, Hebrew — and tries to establish the same five claims about each. The claims are that the feature fires only in its context, fires whenever that context is present, changes the model's output in a matching way, is not just a neuron in disguise, and turns up again in a separately trained model. The specificity argument leans on a hand-built proxy: a cheap score for whether a string looks like the hypothesized context, computed without reference to the model. The paper says outright that these four were chosen for being easy to analyze, not for being typical, which is why the next theme exists.

themes.name: From four features to all of them
themes.summary: Four hand-picked features prove nothing about the population, so the paper turns to measurements over many features and the neurons they are meant to replace. A blinded human rater scores features and neurons on the same rubric; a language model is asked to explain a unit and then predict its activations from that explanation alone; and the reconstruction is spliced back into the transformer to ask how much of the MLP's contribution to loss the features account for. The headline figure is 79%, and the paper attaches its own reasons for reading that number cautiously. It also runs the control that matters most to it — dictionary learning on a randomized transformer — to ask whether the features are about the model or about the data.

themes.name: The same features in a second model
themes.summary: A feature that only exists in one training run says little about neural networks in general. So the paper trains a second one-layer transformer, identical except for its random seed, runs dictionary learning on it separately, and looks for counterparts. Matching is done three ways — by when features fire, by what they do to the logits, and by a combination of the two — and the three do not agree equally well, with agreement on firing running higher than agreement on output effects. This sits after the population evidence because it is the same question asked across models rather than across features.

themes.name: What the features look like together
themes.summary: With thousands of features in hand, the paper stops arguing about individual ones and describes the collection. It sorts them into recurring kinds — features for a whole context, features for one token inside a context, short fixed continuations, memorized phrases — and finds groups that hand off to one another across the token stream like a state machine. Widening the autoencoder does not find new territory but subdivides what was already there, which the paper calls feature splitting and treats as a zoom level rather than a fixed answer. The geometry that comes out of this leads the authors to revise the picture of superposition they started with, and they flag which parts of that revision are still speculation.

themes.name: Judging a training run
themes.summary: The paper trained many autoencoders and had to pick between them, without any single metric that tracks what it cares about. What it does instead is triangulate: look at how sparse the decomposition actually is, how much of the layer's behavior survives substitution, what the histogram of feature firing rates looks like, and — slowest and most trusted — whether the features read as interpretable when a person inspects them. This is the workshop side of the work rather than the argument, which is why it sits near the end. It is also where the paper is most candid that it has no systematic way to tell a good run from a bad one.

themes.name: How to read the charts
themes.summary: This paper argues with a small number of chart shapes, used over and over with different data poured into them. Each one is explained once here: why that shape was chosen, how to read it, and what it would look like if the claim it supports were false. The order follows where a reader meets them — schematics and browser screenshots first, then the per-feature evidence, then the population plots, then the geometry and the training diagnostics. These teach how to read the evidence rather than what it says, so they sit apart from the argument, at the end.

themes.name: Why dictionary learning was the option left
themes.summary: The paper starts from superposition: a layer with 512 neurons may carry many more features by giving each its own direction. More directions than dimensions is overcompleteness, and directions that outnumber dimensions cannot all be orthogonal, so switching one feature on slightly switches others on — interference. That picture is also the reason the authors abandon the other route, which was building models that have no superposition to start with: training the subject model for activation sparsity does not deliver monosemanticity, and a four-feature calculation shows cross-entropy loss prefers a neuron that fires ambiguously on two things to one that fires cleanly on one. What is left is dictionary learning, and the paper picks a deliberately weak solver — a one-hidden-layer autoencoder with an L1 penalty, in place of the classical iterative algorithms it tried and set aside. The argument for weakness is that exact sparse recovery is NP-hard, so a method strong enough to succeed at it might be pulling structure out of the activations that the model itself has no way to read; the penalty is licensed by the older hypothesis that the variables generating natural data are mostly inactive at any moment.

themes.name: The objective, and the numbers used to judge a run
themes.summary: The whole method is one loss: mean squared error between the MLP activation vector and its reconstruction, plus an L1 penalty on the hidden activations. The two terms want opposite things, a coefficient sets the exchange rate between them, and the decoder columns are held to unit norm so the penalty cannot be gamed by shrinking a direction and inflating the activation that rides on it. Those decoder columns are the feature directions, the ReLU hidden values are the feature activations, and the fit as a whole is one concrete way of writing activations as a bias plus a sparse weighted sum of unit vectors — which assumes in advance that the model represents things as directions. The paper has no single number that tracks what it cares about. Training loss cannot be compared across runs with different L1 coefficients, an information-based score rewarded dense solutions, and what survives is a frontier of average features per token against how much of the MLP's loss contribution is recovered, plus a log-scale histogram of how often each feature fires — whose ultralow mode, features firing about once in a million tokens, the authors read as a training artifact rather than as features.

themes.name: An outside yardstick for what a feature responds to
themes.summary: Specificity is the claim that a feature firing implies its hypothesized context is present, and the paper treats it as the more important half of the case, above sensitivity. Establishing it needs a score computed without reference to the feature: a proxy of the form log of P(string given the hypothesis) over P(string), asking how much more likely that text is under a guessed context than under text in general. For a writing system the hard term is inverted with Bayes' rule, so that scoring 'is this Arabic' reduces to checking which Unicode block each character falls in; for character sets like base64 and DNA the conditional is modeled as a uniform draw over the allowed characters. Plotting a feature's activation histogram with every column split by the proxy gives a spectrum rather than one number — the Arabic feature's strongest activations are close to purely Arabic and its weak ones much less so — and the paper argues the strong end is what matters, because a feature's effect on the logits is roughly linear in its activation. Where feature and proxy disagree the paper is often willing to blame the proxy, and says so plainly: the base64 feature correlates only 0.38 with its own yardstick, and hexadecimal strings are counted as base64 by a proxy that is simply too broad.

themes.name: Evidence that a feature changes what the model does
themes.summary: In a one-layer model a feature's effect on the output logits is close to linear in its activation, so a single vector with one entry per vocabulary token — the logit weight — can stand for what firing does, once layer norm is approximated as a fixed projection plus a diagonal scaling. Ablation then means subtracting only the component along the feature's own dictionary direction, leaving every other feature's contribution to that activation vector intact, and doing so lowers the model's predicted probability on Arabic-script tokens across a passage. Holding the feature's activation at a high value and sampling turns the model's continuation into Arabic, which the paper offers against the worry that dictionary learning is recovering correlations in the dataset rather than anything the model computes. The direction is spread over 27 of the 512 neurons, and the neuron whose activations track it most closely fires on a grab-bag of non-English languages, so the decomposition did not simply hand back a neuron under a new name. None of these effects were inputs to the fit, since the autoencoder saw MLP activations only — which is the paper's structural reason for treating an interpretable logit weight as evidence rather than as something the training produced.

themes.name: The same features in a second model
themes.summary: To ask whether a feature is a fact about the model rather than about one training run, the paper trains a second one-layer transformer with the same architecture, data and hyperparameters, differing only in random seed, and runs dictionary learning on it separately. Features are matched by taking the highest Pearson correlation of activations over 40 million dataset examples, and the Arabic feature comes back in the second dictionary. Across the whole population the median match is 0.72 for features against 0.46 for neurons, which is the paper's main quantitative claim here. Agreement on when matched features fire is higher than agreement on what they do, since logit weight similarity is lower — two features can be firing on the same tokens while writing differently to the output. Weighting a feature's logit effects by whether it was actually active and by the token that actually came next brings much of that agreement back.

sections.title: Comparing features between two one-layer transformers

themes.name: Whether any of it holds for features in general
themes.summary: The four features studied in detail were picked because they were easy to analyze rather than because they are typical, and the paper says so before turning to the population of all features. Judging a unit only by its top-activating examples flatters it, so the annotator instead samples from eleven evenly spaced bands across each unit's activation range. Blinded scoring on a 0–14 rubric gives a median of 12 for features and 0 for neurons, and an automated version — where a language model writes an explanation and then predicts activations from that explanation alone, with no other channel from the activations — puts features ahead of neurons too, 74% against 58% on logit-weight questions. Two corrections cut the other way. Features from a randomized transformer initially score slightly higher than the real ones on the automated activation measure, and importance weighting, which is the principled fix for the non-random sampling of scored examples, collapses the scores toward zero — because with feature densities between one in a thousand and one in a million, predicting zero everywhere is nearly right. The paper also notes that most real activations fall in the low bands, which are exactly the bands that score worst.

themes.name: What the dictionary turns up
themes.summary: Making the autoencoder wider does not send features off to new parts of activation space; it splits the ones already there, so a single base64 feature in the 512-unit dictionary becomes three in the 4,096-unit one, separating letters, digits and base64 that decodes to readable text. The features that appear fall into recurring kinds: context features spanning a whole stretch of text, token-in-context features firing on one token only in one setting, and assemblies where one feature raises the probability of tokens that then make the next feature fire — four of which hand off to each other to generate valid HTML. Some of that behavior belongs to the tokenizer rather than the model, since byte-pair encoding splits one Arabic or Hebrew character into a prefix byte and a suffix byte, which is what the two-node loops are built out of. The hundreds of token-in-context features leave a question the paper cannot settle: whether the transformer really uses a local code, one unit per combination of properties, or whether the L1 penalty imposes one on a representation that was compositional. The geometry adds a separate complication, because conceptually related features sit at small angles to each other in tight clusters rather than spreading evenly, which the paper says its inherited toy picture of superposition does not predict.
